label: Parallel speedup and its limits
lesson:
# Parallel speedup and its limits

Parallel hardware speeds up EDA engines only as far as their serial parts allow. Amdahl's and Gustafson's laws quantify this for fixed and growing problems, and the elimination tree of a sparse factorization shows where a direct solver's parallelism actually comes from. Together they let a tool designer predict scaling before buying hardware.

## Amdahl's law for a fixed problem

If a fraction $p$ of a program's single-thread run time parallelizes perfectly over $N$ processors and the rest is serial,
$$S(N) = \frac{1}{(1 - p) + p/N}, \qquad \lim_{N \to \infty} S = \frac{1}{1 - p}.$$
A transient simulation spending 90% of its time in device evaluation and solves, and 10% in serial bookkeeping, gets $S(16) = 1/(0.1 + 0.05625) = 6.4$ and can never exceed 10.

The lesson for engine design is that the serial fraction must shrink as hardware grows: timestep control, convergence checks, output writing and any single-threaded phase become the bottleneck. Profiling the serial fraction is the first step in any parallelization effort.

## Gustafson scaling for growing problems

Often the problem grows with the machine: a larger power grid or a finer thermal mesh. If, in the parallel run on $N$ processors, a fraction $p$ of the time is parallel work, the same work would take $(1 - p) + pN$ times as long on one processor, so the scaled speedup is
$$S = (1 - p) + pN.$$
With $p = 0.95$ and $N = 64$: $S = 0.05 + 60.8 = 60.85$.

The two laws do not conflict; they answer different questions, strong scaling (same problem, faster) and weak scaling (bigger problem, same time). EDA has both needs: faster turnaround on a fixed design, and full-chip analysis that used to require partitioning. Communication cost, not just serial code, usually limits weak scaling in distributed solvers.

## Parallelism in the elimination tree

For a sparse Cholesky factor, the elimination tree has parent$(j)$ = the row index of the first off-diagonal nonzero in column $j$ of $L$. Column $j$ can be factored once all its descendants are done, and columns in disjoint subtrees are independent. With unit work per column, the tree height is the critical path, and the speedup is at most $n/\text{height}$.

Example: 8 columns with parent = 3, 3, 4, 8, 6, 7, 8 for columns 1 to 7. The longest chain is 1 or 2, 3, 4, 8: height 4 columns, while 5, 6, 7, 8 is also 4. Speedup at most $8/4 = 2$. A tridiagonal matrix in natural order gives a path, height $n$, no parallelism; nested dissection gives a short, bushy tree whose independent subtrees run concurrently, which is why parallel sparse solvers use it.

## Going deeper

Amdahl, "Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities", AFIPS (1967); Gustafson, "Reevaluating Amdahl's law", Communications of the ACM (1988); Liu, "The role of elimination trees in sparse factorization", SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. (1990).

problems.q: A transient simulation spends 53 percent of its single-thread time in device evaluation and the sparse solve, which parallelize perfectly, and the rest in serial bookkeeping. By Amdahl's law, what speedup do 16 threads give? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: $S = 1/((1 - p) + p/N) = 1/(0.47 + 0.53/16) = 1.99$; the limit for infinite threads is 2.13.

problems.q: A transient simulation spends 57 percent of its single-thread time in device evaluation and the sparse solve, which parallelize perfectly, and the rest in serial bookkeeping. By Amdahl's law, what speedup do 16 threads give? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: $S = 1/((1 - p) + p/N) = 1/(0.43 + 0.57/16) = 2.15$; the limit for infinite threads is 2.33.

problems.q: A transient simulation spends 60 percent of its single-thread time in device evaluation and the sparse solve, which parallelize perfectly, and the rest in serial bookkeeping. By Amdahl's law, what speedup do 8 threads give? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: $S = 1/((1 - p) + p/N) = 1/(0.4 + 0.6/8) = 2.11$; the limit for infinite threads is 2.5.

problems.q: A power-grid analysis is weak-scaled: the grid grows with the number of nodes so each of 8 processors keeps the same share. In the parallel run, 88 percent of the time is parallel work. By Gustafson's law, what is the scaled speedup? Round to 2 decimal places.

A power-grid analysis is weak-scaled: the grid grows with the number of nodes so each of 8 processors keeps the same share. In the parallel run, 69 percent of the time is parallel work. By Gustafson's law, what is the scaled speedup? Round to 2 decimal places.

A power-grid analysis is weak-scaled: the grid grows with the number of nodes so each of 1024 processors keeps the same share. In the parallel run, 84 percent of the time is parallel work. By Gustafson's law, what is the scaled speedup? Round to 2 decimal places.

The elimination tree of a sparse Cholesky factor on columns 1 to 10 has parent(j) = 3, 3, 6, 8, 6, 7, 9, 9, 10 for j = 1, ..., 9 (column 10 is the root). Each column takes one unit of time and a column can be factored once all its children are done. What is the shortest possible factorization time with unlimited processors (the tree height, counting columns)?
problems.e: The critical path is the longest leaf-to-root chain: 6 columns, so the speedup is at most 10/6.

problems.q: The elimination tree of a sparse Cholesky factor on columns 1 to 10 has parent(j) = 5, 4, 6, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 for j = 1, ..., 9 (column 10 is the root). Each column takes one unit of time and a column can be factored once all its children are done. What is the shortest possible factorization time with unlimited processors (the tree height, counting columns)?
problems.e: The critical path is the longest leaf-to-root chain: 7 columns, so the speedup is at most 10/7.

problems.q: The elimination tree of a sparse Cholesky factor on columns 1 to 7 has parent(j) = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 for j = 1, ..., 6 (column 7 is the root). Each column takes one unit of time and a column can be factored once all its children are done. What is the shortest possible factorization time with unlimited processors (the tree height, counting columns)?
problems.e: The critical path is the longest leaf-to-root chain: 7 columns, so the speedup is at most 7/7.

label: Reduction order and reproducibility
lesson:
# Reduction order and reproducibility

Floating-point addition is not associative, so a parallel sum gives slightly different answers depending on how it is split across threads. In an EDA engine those last-bit differences can change a Newton iteration count, a timestep decision or a placement move, making runs irreproducible. Designing reductions for determinism is part of building a trustworthy numerical kernel.

## Floating-point addition is not associative

IEEE single precision has a 24-bit significand, so the spacing of representable numbers near $2^{24} = 16777216$ is 2. Rounding is to nearest, ties to even. Then
$$(2^{24} + 1) + 1 = 2^{24} + 1 = 2^{24},$$
because each $+1$ lands exactly halfway and rounds to the even neighbour $2^{24}$. But $2^{24} + (1 + 1) = 2^{24} + 2 = 16777218$, exactly representable.

In double precision the same effect appears at $2^{53}$, and partially whenever magnitudes differ widely: adding a small current to a large one discards the small one's low-order bits. Order matters whenever terms of different magnitude are summed, which is every KCL residual and every dot product in a Krylov solver.

## Computing a sum in two orders

Sum $1, 1, 2^{24}, 1, 1$ in float32 left to right: $1 + 1 = 2$, $2 + 2^{24} = 16777218$, then $+1$ gives a tie between 16777218 and 16777220, resolved to even significand: 16777220; $+1$ again ties between 16777220 and 16777222 and rounds to 16777220. The result is 16777220, equal to the exact sum by luck of the ties.

With the order $2^{24}, 1, 1, 1, 1$: each $+1$ rounds back to $2^{24}$, and the result is 16777216, off by 4. A parallel reduction whose thread count or scheduling changes between runs takes different orders, so it can return either answer. GPU atomic additions make the order depend on timing and are inherently nondeterministic.

## Making parallel results reproducible

Error bounds depend on order too. Recursive left-to-right summation of $n$ terms has error at most about $(n - 1)u\sum|x_i|$; pairwise (tree) summation has at most about $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil u\sum|x_i|$. For $n = 10^6$ that is a factor $999999/20 = 50{,}000$ smaller worst-case bound.

Reproducibility needs a fixed order, not just accuracy. Common designs: a fixed reduction tree independent of thread count; deterministic partitioning of work with results combined in index order; compensated (Kahan) summation, which shrinks the dependence on order; and exact or reproducible accumulators that give bit-identical results regardless of order. Each costs some speed. Engines typically offer a deterministic mode for golden tests and signoff and a faster mode for exploration, and say clearly which is which.

## Going deeper

Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (2nd ed., SIAM, 2002), chapter 4; Demmel and Nguyen, "Parallel reproducible summation", IEEE Trans. Computers (2015).

problems.q: In IEEE single precision (24-bit significand, round to nearest even), compute $(2^{25} + 2) + 2$ exactly as the hardware would, rounding after each addition. What is the result? ($2^{25} = 33554432$.)
problems.e: Near $2^{25}$ the spacing of float32 numbers is 4, so small additions round to the nearest representable value at each step; the result is 33554432.

problems.q: In IEEE single precision (24-bit significand, round to nearest even), compute $(2^{25} + 3) + 3$ exactly as the hardware would, rounding after each addition. What is the result? ($2^{25} = 33554432$.)
problems.e: Near $2^{25}$ the spacing of float32 numbers is 4, so small additions round to the nearest representable value at each step; the result is 33554440.

problems.q: In IEEE single precision (24-bit significand, round to nearest even), compute $(2^{25} + 3) + 1$ exactly as the hardware would, rounding after each addition. What is the result? ($2^{25} = 33554432$.)
problems.e: Near $2^{25}$ the spacing of float32 numbers is 4, so small additions round to the nearest representable value at each step; the result is 33554436.

problems.q: Partial sums from 4 threads arrive in the order 3, 3, 33554432, 2 and are added left to right in float32 (24-bit significand, round to nearest even). What is the final sum?
problems.e: Once the running sum reaches 33554432, each small term is at most one ulp and may be rounded away; the left-to-right float32 sum is 33554440, while the exact sum is 33554440.

problems.q: Partial sums from 6 threads arrive in the order 1, 1, 33554432, 3, 2, 3 and are added left to right in float32 (24-bit significand, round to nearest even). What is the final sum?
problems.e: Once the running sum reaches 33554432, each small term is at most one ulp and may be rounded away; the left-to-right float32 sum is 33554444, while the exact sum is 33554442.

problems.q: Partial sums from 4 threads arrive in the order 3, 33554432, 2, 2 and are added left to right in float32 (24-bit significand, round to nearest even). What is the final sum?
problems.e: Once the running sum reaches 33554432, each small term is at most one ulp and may be rounded away; the left-to-right float32 sum is 33554440, while the exact sum is 33554439.

problems.q: Summing n = 4096 terms, the first-order error bound is $(n - 1)u\sum|x_i|$ for left-to-right summation and $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil u\sum|x_i|$ for pairwise (tree) summation. By what factor is the pairwise bound smaller? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $(n - 1)/\lceil\log_2 n\rceil = 4095/12 = 341.2$. A fixed reduction tree is both more accurate and reproducible.

problems.q: Summing n = 100000 terms, the first-order error bound is $(n - 1)u\sum|x_i|$ for left-to-right summation and $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil u\sum|x_i|$ for pairwise (tree) summation. By what factor is the pairwise bound smaller? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $(n - 1)/\lceil\log_2 n\rceil = 99999/17 = 5882.3$. A fixed reduction tree is both more accurate and reproducible.

problems.q: Summing n = 1000000 terms, the first-order error bound is $(n - 1)u\sum|x_i|$ for left-to-right summation and $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil u\sum|x_i|$ for pairwise (tree) summation. By what factor is the pairwise bound smaller? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $(n - 1)/\lceil\log_2 n\rceil = 999999/20 = 49999.9$. A fixed reduction tree is both more accurate and reproducible.

label: Numerical kernels as an immutable core
lesson:
# Numerical kernels as an immutable core

In an agent-first EDA engine, the numerical kernels are the immutable core: the code every analysis trusts and every agent calls but rarely edits. Deciding precisely what belongs in that core for a simulator, IR-drop or thermal solver, and what is policy, parameter or hook, is the design decision that lets agents customize solvers safely.

## What belongs in the solver core

The core holds what defines correctness: sparse factorization and triangular solves, SpMV, the Krylov recurrences, the integration formulas and their LTE estimators, the Newton update, and the definitions behind every reported number, such as what a residual is and what "converged" means. A downstream timer or signoff check reads a converged waveform as a contract; if the meaning of the tolerance changed silently, every result would change meaning with it.

Two practical rules follow. First, the hot loops stay inside the core and the seams around it are coarse, called once per solve or per batch, so the compiler can inline and vectorize. Second, a change to the core, say a new LTE formula or a different residual scaling, is a Tier 3 change: it needs a human-approved diff and a full regression, because it alters the accuracy contract of every analysis.

## Policies, parameters and hooks around a solver

Around the core sit three easier-to-change layers. Policy: which ordering (AMD, nested dissection, Markowitz), which preconditioner, which integration method among those the core provides, which damping or limiting strategy, which timestep controller. Parameters: reltol, abstol, vntol, pivot threshold, GMRES restart length, maximum Newton iterations, fast or accurate mode. Hooks: per-iteration residual norms, the node with the largest update, accepted and rejected steps, pivot growth, condition estimates.

Classifying requests by layer is the daily work. "Use BDF2 for this PLL" is a policy choice; "tighten reltol to 1e-4" is a parameter; "let the agent see which node fails Newton" is a hook. None of them touches the core, so none needs a recompile of the kernel, and most need only a configuration change.

## The determinism contract of a kernel

Agents compare runs: a baseline against a candidate, a golden result against a new build. That only works if the same inputs and settings give the same answer. So the core promises determinism: fixed reduction orders, no hidden global state, explicit seeds for anything random, and results independent of thread scheduling.

Fast paths may relax this, for example GPU atomic-add reductions, but then the engine offers two declared modes, a deterministic one for comparisons and signoff and a nondeterministic one for exploration where only rough rankings matter. A reordering of floating-point operations for speed changes results in the last digits; the release process must then show tolerance-based agreement with golden results and determinism within the new version, since bitwise equality across the change is impossible.

## Going deeper

The four-layer engine model and change tiers in docs/eda/agent-first-concepts.md of this repository; Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (2nd ed., SIAM, 2002), chapter 4 on summation order.

problems.q:
Which property of the solver core must every change preserve, because downstream engines and golden tests depend on it?

A) The ordering chosen for every matrix

B) The exact number of Newton iterations on every design

C) The wall-clock time of each solve

D) The meaning of the residual and the convergence test, so a reported tolerance always means the same thing
problems.a: The meaning of the residual and the convergence test, so a reported tolerance always means the same thing
problems.e: Iteration counts and orderings may change; the contract that a converged solution satisfies a stated residual tolerance may not.

problems.q:
Why keep the hot numerical kernels (SpMV, triangular solve, element evaluation) inside the core rather than behind fine-grained plug-in calls?

A) The kernels change too often to be core

B) Per-entry calls across a plug-in boundary block inlining and vectorization and would dominate run time

C) Plug-ins cannot perform floating-point arithmetic

D) Agents cannot call core code
problems.a: Per-entry calls across a plug-in boundary block inlining and vectorization and would dominate run time
problems.e: Seams should be coarse, per solve or per batch, so the compiler can optimize the inner loops.

problems.q:
An engineer proposes to change the local truncation error estimator of the transient engine. Where does that change live?

A) In the core: it changes the accuracy contract of every transient result

B) In the strategy layer, as a new ordering

C) In an observation hook

D) In the parameters, as a new reltol
problems.a: In the core: it changes the accuracy contract of every transient result
problems.e: The LTE formula decides which steps are accepted, so it defines result accuracy; editing it is a core change needing approval and full regression.

problems.q:
A request reads: tighten reltol from 1e-3 to 1e-4 for a precision ADC block. Which layer handles it?

A) Parameters: a configuration value with no recompile

B) A new observation hook

C) A new plug-in

D) The immutable core
problems.a: Parameters: a configuration value with no recompile
problems.e: Tolerances are parameters; changing them changes run time and accuracy without touching code.

problems.q:
A damping strategy that limits per-device junction voltage changes is to be swapped for a global line search. Which layer is that?

A) The immutable core

B) Parameters

C) Strategy: both are policies around the same Newton update

D) An observation hook
problems.a: Strategy: both are policies around the same Newton update
problems.e: How to scale or limit the Newton step is a policy decision; the Newton update and Jacobian assembly stay in the core.

problems.q:
A request reads: tighten reltol from 1e-3 to 1e-4 for a precision ADC block. Which layer handles it?

A) The immutable core

B) A new observation hook

C) Parameters: a configuration value with no recompile

D) A new plug-in
problems.a: Parameters: a configuration value with no recompile
problems.e: Tolerances are parameters; changing them changes run time and accuracy without touching code.

problems.q:
Where should a seedable random choice inside a solver (say, a random restart vector for an eigensolver) get its seed?

A) From the system clock

B) From an explicit parameter recorded with the run, so the result can be reproduced

C) From uninitialized memory

D) From the thread scheduler
problems.a: From an explicit parameter recorded with the run, so the result can be reproduced
problems.e: Everything stochastic must be seeded explicitly so that runs reproduce and diffs are meaningful.

problems.q:
Where should a seedable random choice inside a solver (say, a random restart vector for an eigensolver) get its seed?

A) From the system clock

B) From an explicit parameter recorded with the run, so the result can be reproduced

C) From the thread scheduler

D) From uninitialized memory
problems.a: From an explicit parameter recorded with the run, so the result can be reproduced
problems.e: Everything stochastic must be seeded explicitly so that runs reproduce and diffs are meaningful.

problems.q:
A GPU solver offers a deterministic mode and a faster mode with atomic-add reductions. When should an agent loop use the deterministic mode?

A) Only when the matrix is unsymmetric

B) Only for designs under 1000 nodes

C) Whenever results are compared against a baseline or golden reference

D) Never, since the fast mode is always within tolerance
problems.a: Whenever results are compared against a baseline or golden reference
problems.e: Comparisons need reproducible numbers; the nondeterministic fast mode can be used for exploration where only rough rankings matter.

label: Seams for solvers and preconditioners
prereqs: Numerical kernels as an immutable core
lesson:
# Seams for solvers and preconditioners

A seam is the narrow, stable interface where new behaviour plugs into an engine without touching its core. For numerical engines the most valuable seams are around the linear solver and the preconditioner, because that is where customers' matrices differ most. Where the seam sits, and what context it passes, decides whether solver changes are configuration, plug-ins or core edits.

## The linear solver and preconditioner seams

A good linear-solver seam mirrors the structure of sparse direct solvers: analyze(pattern), factor(values), solve(rhs). Splitting analysis from factorization exposes the reuse that matters in simulation: the pattern is fixed across Newton iterations and timesteps, so a solver plug-in orders once and refactors many times. A preconditioner seam is setup(A) and apply(r), where apply returns an approximation to $A^{-1}r$ once per Krylov iteration.

Calls are coarse, per matrix or per solve, never per entry, so the plug-in owns its inner loops and the core's performance is preserved. Plug-ins receive plain data structures (CSR arrays, vectors), keep no hidden global state, and are deterministic given their inputs. A plug-in that caches state between calls without declaring it breaks reproducibility and golden tests.

## What context the seam must expose

A plug-in can only choose well if the seam tells it what it is solving. Useful context: structural flags (symmetric, positive definite, M-matrix), so it can pick Cholesky or CG over LU or GMRES; whether the pattern changed since the last call and how much the values changed, so it can reuse a factorization or preconditioner; the outer Newton tolerance and current nonlinear residual, so an inner iterative solve is only as accurate as needed (inexact Newton); and domain metadata such as node coordinates and metal layers, so a power-grid preconditioner can coarsen by layer.

Context should be data, not callbacks into the core. Missing context forces plug-ins to guess, for instance re-analysing every call or solving every system to $10^{-14}$, which wastes the speed the seam was meant to unlock.

## Classifying solver change requests by tier

Tier 1 is configuration: switch the IR-drop preconditioner from Jacobi to incomplete Cholesky, which the tool ships; change the GMRES restart from 30 to 60; tighten a tolerance. Tier 2 is a plug-in at an existing seam: a block-Jacobi preconditioner whose blocks are power-grid layers, or a new ordering for a family of analog netlists. Tier 3 is a core edit: declaring Newton convergence on the residual alone, changing the LTE estimator, altering how gmin is applied.

The tier is a test of the seams. If most requests over a year needed Tier 3, behaviour that varies is trapped in the core and the seam is in the wrong place. The right response is to move that variability behind an interface once, under human review, so that future requests of that kind land in Tier 1 or 2.

## Going deeper

Davis, "Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems" (SIAM, 2006), chapter 1 on the analyze-factor-solve structure; Balay et al., "PETSc users manual" (Argonne National Laboratory), on KSP and PC interfaces as a model of solver and preconditioner seams.

problems.q:
Why should the linear-solver seam separate the symbolic analysis call from the numeric factorization call?

A) Some solvers have no symbolic phase, so it must be hidden

B) Numeric factorization does not need the pattern

C) The pattern is fixed across Newton iterations and timesteps, so the ordering is computed once and the numeric factorization repeated

D) Symbolic analysis is the cheapest step
problems.a: The pattern is fixed across Newton iterations and timesteps, so the ordering is computed once and the numeric factorization repeated
problems.e: Separating the phases exposes the reuse that makes sparse direct solvers fast in simulation.

problems.q:
A preconditioner seam offers setup(A) and apply(r). What does apply(r) return?

A) The residual r - Ax

B) The exact solution of Ax = r

C) An approximation of A^-1 r, used once per Krylov iteration

D) The condition number of A
problems.a: An approximation of A^-1 r, used once per Krylov iteration
problems.e: A preconditioner applies an approximate inverse; the Krylov method stays responsible for convergence.

problems.q:
A plug-in preconditioner keeps a hidden global cache between calls. Why is that a seam violation?

A) Caches always increase memory use

B) Results then depend on call history, which breaks determinism and makes golden tests unreliable

C) The compiler cannot compile global variables

D) Global variables are slower to read
problems.a: Results then depend on call history, which breaks determinism and makes golden tests unreliable
problems.e: Seams should pass plain data and keep no hidden state, so the same inputs always give the same outputs.

problems.q:
Which context should the solver seam expose so a plug-in can choose between Cholesky and LU?

A) The output waveform file path

B) The name of the designer

C) Whether the matrix is symmetric and positive definite (for example, a pure RC or power-grid matrix)

D) The number of netlist comments
problems.a: Whether the matrix is symmetric and positive definite (for example, a pure RC or power-grid matrix)
problems.e: Structure hints decide the algorithm: SPD matrices allow Cholesky or CG; general MNA matrices need LU or GMRES.

problems.q:
A power-grid preconditioner wants to coarsen by metal layer. What must the seam provide beyond the matrix?

A) The timing constraints

B) The die cost

C) A map from unknowns to grid layers and coordinates

D) The SPICE netlist text
problems.a: A map from unknowns to grid layers and coordinates
problems.e: Geometric or structural metadata lets a plug-in build better hierarchies than it could infer from matrix entries alone.

problems.q:
Which context should the solver seam expose so a plug-in can choose between Cholesky and LU?

A) The name of the designer

B) The output waveform file path

C) The number of netlist comments

D) Whether the matrix is symmetric and positive definite (for example, a pure RC or power-grid matrix)
problems.a: Whether the matrix is symmetric and positive definite (for example, a pure RC or power-grid matrix)
problems.e: Structure hints decide the algorithm: SPD matrices allow Cholesky or CG; general MNA matrices need LU or GMRES.

problems.q:
A team wants a block-Jacobi preconditioner whose blocks are the power-grid layers. It does not exist yet. Which tier?

A) Tier 2: a new plug-in behind the preconditioner seam

B) Tier 3: a core edit

C) No change: Jacobi already covers it

D) Tier 1: a configuration value
problems.a: Tier 2: a new plug-in behind the preconditioner seam
problems.e: It is new code, but it fits the existing setup/apply seam, so the core stays untouched.

problems.q:
A team wants a block-Jacobi preconditioner whose blocks are the power-grid layers. It does not exist yet. Which tier?

A) No change: Jacobi already covers it

B) Tier 1: a configuration value

C) Tier 3: a core edit

D) Tier 2: a new plug-in behind the preconditioner seam
problems.a: Tier 2: a new plug-in behind the preconditioner seam
problems.e: It is new code, but it fits the existing setup/apply seam, so the core stays untouched.

problems.q:
Over a year, most solver change requests have needed Tier 3 core edits. What does that indicate?

A) The core is well designed

B) Plug-ins are too powerful

C) The seams are in the wrong place: behaviour that varies is trapped inside the core

D) Customers should stop requesting changes
problems.a: The seams are in the wrong place: behaviour that varies is trapped inside the core
problems.e: A good seam makes the common change a configuration or plug-in; frequent core edits signal that the variable part is not exposed.

label: Differential tests for solver changes
prereqs: Numerical kernels as an immutable core
lesson:
# Differential tests for solver changes

Every change to a numerical engine, by an agent or a person, must be proven before promotion. For solvers the proof has a specific shape: backward-error and residual checks that are independent of conditioning, forward comparisons whose tolerances scale with the condition number, and golden circuits whose answers are known. Getting these right is what makes automated solver edits safe.

## Residual and backward-error checks

The normwise backward error of a computed solution $\hat x$ is
$$\eta = \frac{\|b - A\hat x\|}{\|A\|\,\|\hat x\| + \|b\|}.$$
It is the smallest relative perturbation of $A$ and $b$ for which $\hat x$ is exact, and it does not depend on $\kappa$. A backward-stable direct solver in double precision gives $\eta$ near $10^{-16}$ times a modest factor; an iterative solver gives $\eta$ near its stopping tolerance.

Example: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, $b = (6, 7)$, exact $x = (1, 2)$, computed $\hat x = (1.0001, 1.9999)$. Then $r = b - A\hat x = (-0.0003, 0.0002)$, $\|r\|_\infty = 3 \times 10^{-4}$, $\|A\|_\infty = 5$, $\|\hat x\|_\infty = 1.9999$, $\|b\|_\infty = 7$: $\eta = 3 \times 10^{-4}/17.0 = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$. For a direct solver that is a failure.

## Tolerances that respect conditioning

Two correct solvers can return different answers. If each meets a relative residual tolerance $\tau$, each forward error is bounded by about $\kappa\tau$, so their solutions may differ by up to about $2\kappa\tau$. With $\kappa = 10^7$ and $\tau = 10^{-10}$, a relative difference of $10^{-3}$ is consistent; a difference of $10^{-1}$ is not, and one solver is wrong.

So a differential test comparing solutions must scale its tolerance with a condition estimate, or it will flag correct changes on ill-conditioned cases and miss real bugs on well-conditioned ones. A residual or backward-error check needs no such scaling, which is why it is the first gate. Waveform comparisons follow the same logic: compare at common sample times, with reltol and abstol bands, because adaptive timestep selection differs between versions.

## Golden circuits and what must not move

A golden suite for a solver mixes cases with known answers and cases that stress numerics: an RC step response against the analytic exponential; a diode DC point against an independent high-precision solve; an IR-drop grid with an independently verified worst-node drop; deliberately ill-conditioned matrices; stiff and oscillatory transients to catch damping or ringing changes.

Beyond accuracy, the differential report records cost as QoR: Newton iterations, timesteps accepted and rejected, Krylov iterations, factorization fill and memory. A plug-in that matches every waveform but doubles Newton iterations is a regression to review, not a pass. Small designs are not enough: promotion needs the QoR baseline on representative large designs, where scaling problems in fill or iteration count appear.

## Going deeper

Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (2nd ed., SIAM, 2002), chapters 1 and 7 on backward error; Rigal and Gaches, "On the compatibility of a given solution with the data of a linear system", J. ACM (1967).

A) $2.4 \times 10^{-4}$

B) $2.18 \times 10^{-5}$

C) $7.5 \times 10^{-6}$

A) $1.5 \times 10^{-3}$

B) $6 \times 10^{-3}$

C) $2 \times 10^{-3}$

problems.e: $\|r\|_\infty = 0.048$, $\|A\|_\infty = 12$, $\|\hat x\|_\infty = 1.996$, $\|b\|_\infty = 8$. A stable solver in double precision gives $\eta$ near $10^{-16}$; this one is far above, so the test fails.

An old and a new linear solver each meet a relative residual tolerance of $10^{-10}$ on a matrix with $\kappa \approx 10^{8}$. Their solutions differ by a relative amount $6 \times 10^{-3}$. What should the differential test conclude?

A) Inconsistent: the difference exceeds the roughly $2 \times 10^{-2}$ that conditioning allows, so one solver is wrong

B) Consistent: any difference is acceptable once both residuals pass

C) Inconsistent: the solutions must agree to $10^{-10}$, the residual tolerance

D) Consistent: forward errors of up to about $\kappa \cdot 10^{-10}$ each are allowed, so a difference up to about $2 \times 10^{-2}$ is expected
problems.a: Consistent: forward errors of up to about $\kappa \cdot 10^{-10}$ each are allowed, so a difference up to about $2 \times 10^{-2}$ is expected
problems.e: Each solution's relative error is bounded by kappa times its relative residual, so the two may differ by about the sum of those bounds; this difference is within it.

problems.q:
An old and a new linear solver each meet a relative residual tolerance of $10^{-11}$ on a matrix with $\kappa \approx 10^{3}$. Their solutions differ by a relative amount $1.6 \times 10^{-6}$. What should the differential test conclude?

A) Consistent: forward errors of up to about $\kappa \cdot 10^{-11}$ each are allowed, so a difference up to about $2 \times 10^{-8}$ is expected

B) Inconsistent: the difference exceeds the roughly $2 \times 10^{-8}$ that conditioning allows, so one solver is wrong

C) Consistent: any difference is acceptable once both residuals pass

D) Inconsistent: the solutions must agree to $10^{-11}$, the residual tolerance
problems.a: Inconsistent: the difference exceeds the roughly $2 \times 10^{-8}$ that conditioning allows, so one solver is wrong
problems.e: The bound kappa times the residual tolerance, summed over both solvers, is far smaller than the observed difference, so at least one solution is wrong.

problems.q:
An old and a new linear solver each meet a relative residual tolerance of $10^{-9}$ on a matrix with $\kappa \approx 10^{4}$. Their solutions differ by a relative amount $1.4 \times 10^{-5}$. What should the differential test conclude?

A) Inconsistent: the solutions must agree to $10^{-9}$, the residual tolerance

B) Consistent: any difference is acceptable once both residuals pass

C) Consistent: forward errors of up to about $\kappa \cdot 10^{-9}$ each are allowed, so a difference up to about $2 \times 10^{-5}$ is expected

problems.a: Consistent: forward errors of up to about $\kappa \cdot 10^{-9}$ each are allowed, so a difference up to about $2 \times 10^{-5}$ is expected

problems.q:
A solver change passes all golden tests but was only run on small designs. What must still be shown before promotion?

A) Nothing more, because golden tests passed

B) That the change compiles on one machine

C) That the change is short

D) Results and run time on representative large designs from the QoR baseline
problems.a: Results and run time on representative large designs from the QoR baseline
problems.e: Scaling behaviour (fill, iteration counts, memory) appears on large designs; promotion needs the baseline comparison too.

problems.q:
A differential test compares two transient engines by their waveforms at every timestep of the run. Why does that fail spuriously?

A) Waveforms cannot be compared at all

B) The comparison must use bitwise equality

C) Transient engines always pick the same timesteps

D) The engines choose different timesteps, so waveforms must be compared at common times by interpolation or at fixed sample points
problems.a: The engines choose different timesteps, so waveforms must be compared at common times by interpolation or at fixed sample points
problems.e: Adaptive step control makes time grids differ; comparisons must align the grids before applying tolerances.

problems.q:
Why should a solver golden suite contain deliberately ill-conditioned matrices?

A) They are needed to test the netlist parser

B) A change that is harmless on well-conditioned cases can lose many digits when kappa is large

C) They make every solver agree exactly

D) Ill-conditioned matrices run faster
problems.a: A change that is harmless on well-conditioned cases can lose many digits when kappa is large
problems.e: Stability problems show up only under ill-conditioning; well-conditioned tests hide them.

lesson:
# GPU solvers inside agent loops

Agents exploring power-grid straps, decap placements or thermal floorplans issue hundreds of similar solves. GPU solvers make that loop fast, but only if the loop is organized around how GPUs work: batched, warm-started, bandwidth-bound solves, with a clear rule for when a fast answer is good enough and when to call the accurate engine.

## Batching many small solves

Each independent solve pays fixed costs: symbolic analysis, data transfer, kernel launches. When candidates share a sparsity pattern, those costs can be paid once. With setup $s$ and numeric work $t$ per candidate, $k$ unbatched solves cost $k(s + t)$ and a batch costs about $s + kt$.

Example: $k = 100$ variants of a PDN, $s = 20$ ms, $t = 4$ ms. Unbatched: 2400 ms. Batched: 420 ms, a factor of 5.7. Batching also fills the GPU: a single small solve leaves most of the device idle, while a batch of a hundred keeps it busy. Warm starts help further: consecutive candidates differ slightly, so starting CG from the previous solution makes the initial residual small and cuts iterations, often by a large factor.

## Budgeting candidate evaluations

An agent loop has a time budget. With total time $T$, fixed overhead $F$ (loading the design, building the base matrix), fast-mode cost $t_f$ per candidate, and the requirement that the best $m$ candidates be re-run in the accurate solver at $t_a$ each, the number of fast candidates that fit is
$$N = \left\lfloor\frac{T - F - mt_a}{t_f}\right\rfloor.$$
With $T = 30$ minutes, $F = 60$ s, $t_f = 2$ s, $m = 5$ and $t_a = 120$ s: $N = \lfloor(1800 - 60 - 600)/2\rfloor = 570$.

Forgetting to reserve the accurate re-runs is the common planning error: the loop finds a winner and then has no time to confirm it. The budget also shows the leverage of the fast mode: halving $t_f$ doubles the exploration.

## When to recurse to the accurate solver

A fast mode (FP32, loose tolerance, coarse mesh, reduced model) has an error band $e$. The agent recurses to the accurate engine when the fast answer cannot decide: two candidates closer than $2e$; a candidate within $e$ of a constraint limit, such as 49 mV against a 50 mV IR-drop limit with a 2 mV band; or a design unlike the one on which the band was measured, since error bands of fast modes are empirical and must be re-measured on a new design class.

And it always recurses before signoff. The fast mode guides exploration; the accurate engine, with validated tolerances in its deterministic mode, produces the numbers a human approves. Using fast-mode numbers as the reward for a learning agent invites reward hacking: the agent finds layouts the fast mode scores well and the accurate solver does not.

## Going deeper

Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop, docs/eda/agent-first-concepts.md of this repository; Williams, Waterman and Patterson, "Roofline: an insightful visual performance model for multicore architectures", Communications of the ACM (2009).

A) Switch to forward Euler

C) None: numerical error does not depend on the design

D) The accurate solver will become slower
problems.a: The fast mode's error band may not hold on the new design class, so it must be re-measured against the accurate solver

Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop

lesson:
# Fast and accurate solver modes

Every numerical engine can trade accuracy for speed: looser tolerances, lower precision, coarser meshes, larger timesteps, reduced models. An agent running a continuous modeling loop needs to know exactly what each fast setting buys and costs, how to tell whether a fast result can rank candidates, and when a result must be promoted to the accurate engine.

## Loose tolerances and what they buy

Many fast settings have predictable effects. CG iterations grow like $\ln(2/\varepsilon)$ at fixed $\kappa$, so relaxing the tolerance from $10^{-10}$ to $10^{-4}$ cuts iterations to about $\ln(2 \times 10^4)/\ln(2 \times 10^{10}) = 9.90/23.72 = 0.42$ of the original. Trapezoidal LTE scales like $h^3$, so loosening the timestep tolerance tenfold grows steps by $10^{1/3} = 2.15$ and cuts step count by about that factor. FP32 halves memory traffic for bandwidth-bound kernels, nearly doubling SpMV speed, but loses digits on ill-conditioned matrices.

Coarsening a thermal mesh by 2 in 3D cuts unknowns by 8 and, at the same tolerance, CG iterations by about 2. Each of these is a parameter or policy setting, Tier 1, so an agent can switch modes without touching the core.

## Error budgets for ranking candidates

An agent mostly uses fast results to rank: is layout A better than layout B? If each fast estimate is within $\pm e$ of the accurate value, A's true value can be $e$ higher and B's $e$ lower, so the ranking is trustworthy only if the gap exceeds $2e$.

Example: fast worst-case IR drops of 42.1 mV for A and 44.0 mV for B, with $e = 0.8$ mV. The gap 1.9 mV exceeds 1.6 mV, so A really is better. With $e = 1.2$ mV the combined band 2.4 mV exceeds the gap, and the agent must recurse. In practice $e$ is measured: run fast and accurate modes on a sample of candidates of the same design class and record the error distribution, or the rank correlation between the two.

## Promoting a fast result to signoff

Promotion means re-running the chosen candidate in accurate mode: FP64, tight tolerances, full mesh, deterministic reductions, and deciding on those numbers alone. Fast numbers are never reported as signoff results, even with a disclaimer.

Three checks guard the loop. First, the fast mode's error band must have been measured on designs like the current one; a reduced thermal model built for one floorplan can be badly wrong on another. Second, when fast results feed a learning agent's reward, periodically recompute rewards with the accurate engine: an agent that learns layouts the fast mode likes but the accurate engine does not is reward hacking the proxy. Third, keep the fast mode deterministic within itself, so that rankings are reproducible and differences between candidates are real.

## Going deeper

Fast and accurate engines, and tool-grounded reinforcement learning, in docs/eda/agent-first-concepts.md of this repository; Carson and Higham, "Accelerating the solution of linear systems by iterative refinement in three precisions", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. (2018).

B) 23

C) 89

D) 50

E) 85
problems.e: $170 \cdot \ln(2 \cdot 10^{3})/\ln(2 \cdot 10^{11}) = 50$ iterations.

D) No: the gap of 1.5 mV is within the combined error of 1.6 mV, so recurse to the accurate solver

An agent's reward is computed from fast-mode IR drop. Over many iterations it learns layouts whose fast-mode drop is low but whose accurate drop is not. What is this?

A) Reward hacking of the fast proxy; the reward must be periodically checked or computed with the accurate engine

B) Proof that the fast mode is more accurate

C) Normal convergence of the agent

D) A bug in the accurate engine
problems.a: Reward hacking of the fast proxy; the reward must be periodically checked or computed with the accurate engine
problems.e: Optimizing against a proxy finds the proxy's blind spots; grounding the reward in the accurate tool closes the gap.

problems.q:
A reduced-order thermal model is used as the fast mode. What must be checked before trusting its rankings on a new floorplan?

A) That the reduction error on that floorplan, measured against the full model on a few cases, is below the ranking margins

B) That the reduced model has fewer states than the full one

C) Nothing: reduced models are exact at DC

D) That the reduced model runs faster
problems.a: That the reduction error on that floorplan, measured against the full model on a few cases, is below the ranking margins
problems.e: A reduced model is accurate only for the inputs and geometries it was built for; its error must be measured where it is used.

problems.q:

A) A deterministic reduction order

B) Reusing the symbolic analysis

C) A loose iterative-solver tolerance whose error is comparable to the margin

D) Warm starting from the previous solution
problems.a: A loose iterative-solver tolerance whose error is comparable to the margin
problems.e: Solver tolerance directly bounds the error of each estimate; the others save work without adding error.
